text: the lamp in the east window went out again. nobody went to light it.
a woman came up the pit road carrying a lantern with no flame in it. she says it still works.
the bread ran short. the miners didn't complain. that was worse.
something scratched at the shutters until dawn. dawn doesn't come anymore, so it's still scratching.
the smith traded his good hammer for six candles. he says the dark is the bigger job.
two children found a door in the slag heap. the door is fine. it's what they say was behind it.
Foreman's ledger, last entry: Shaft four reopened. Men report the seam is warm to the touch, and that it hums when the lamps are low. Production up. I have told them to keep the lamps high.
A lantern of blackened brass, its glass fogged from the inside. The miners won't carry it. They say it shows you the way out, and that the way out isn't up.
Scratched into the wall of the old chapel, in a careful hand: WE COUNTED THE DAYS UNTIL WE COULDN'T. Below it, in a different hand, the tally continues for another three hundred marks.
Letter, unsent: Mother, the sun is fine here. We see it most days. The work is good and the food is good. I am lying because you would come, and you must not come.
The miners always sing on the way down so the dark knows they're coming. Last shift, the dark sang back.
We stopped counting the dead when the numbers started going down.
Every lamp in town blew out at once, and in the silence I heard the mountain take a breath.
My daughter says the man in the pit asks about me by name. I have never told her my name.
The last sunrise lasted four hours, and we cheered, until the astronomer pointed out it was setting in the east.
We buried him at the bottom of shaft nine, because that's where he asked to go. He asked yesterday.
The council voted to ration lamp oil, then voted again by candlelight because nobody could see the first vote.
Old Brannick says he's survived three cave-ins, a flood and the end of the sun, and the thing that's going to kill him is the new cook. He may be right. Nobody has identified the stew.
The priest insists the sun will return if we are good. The children have been very good for four months now and are starting to ask pointed questions.

Mara keeps the lamp on the corner of Pit Street. It isn't her job. It was her husband's, and then the dark took him on the long shift, and the next evening someone had to climb the ladder, and it was her. Now she does it twice a day, though there's no day anymore, only the bell. People nod to her. She doesn't nod back; she's counting rungs. Thirty-one up, thirty-one down. Some nights the lamp across the square goes out while she's lighting hers, and she stands at the top of the ladder and waits, very still, to see what walks through the dark between them.

The trader came in from the high road with a cart of salted meat and wouldn't say what kind. We bought all of it. The children ate first, then the old ones, then the rest. That night he sat by the furnace and told us there were towns out there with lamps on every street, where the dark kept to itself. We asked why he'd left. He looked at the meat on our plates for a long time before he said he hadn't.
